nodes.question: How do situational influences affect people's acceptability judgments?
nodes.answer: Situational influences can significantly impact acceptability judgments formed with less elaboration, as they are more susceptible to changes in how questions are framed or the context in which they are presented.
nodes.paragraph: Based on the ELM (Petty & Cacioppo, 1986), we argue that when people form acceptability judgements about technologies, these can vary in depth of elaboration, which is likely to impact the stability of acceptability judgements. For novel technologies, people have had fewer opportuni- ties for thinking carefully about their pros and cons. Thus, people likely form their acceptability judge- ments very spontaneously, relying more on heuristics and cues than on detailed elaboration (Daamen et al., 2006; Malone et al., 2010). This likely results in less stable acceptability judgements, as judgements based on less elaboration are more strongly affected by changing situational influences and cues, for instance the way questions are framed or the context in which they are asked (Converse, 1970; Malone et al., 2010). In contrast, people S acceptability judgements regarding established energy technologies such as wind or nuclear energy tend to be based on higher familiarity with the technology, its pros and cons, and more encounters with the technology through media or other exposure (Ashworth et al., 2013; Whitmarsh et al., 2015).

nodes.question: How can metacognitive reasoning affect personal beliefs according to Mezirow?
nodes.answer: Metacognitive reasoning can alter a person's frame of reference, leading to transformations in beliefs and opportunities for societal change.
nodes.paragraph: Mezirow characterizes learning as a process of critical self-reflection, leading to re-evaluating one S perspective to foster a more comprehensive, discerning, and interactive understanding of personal experiences ( 1991 , p. xvi). The process is a form of metacognitive reasoning, which is specifically adult-oriented and can ultimately pave the way for acquiring knowledge and deeper comprehension. Such reasoning can alter a person S frame of reference (i.e., their cognitive framework) and may open opportunities for transforming beliefs, emancipation, and societal change through individual action (Mezirow, 2003 ). According to Mezirow ( 1991 ), learning is transformative when it changes behaviour or a new form of action. This type of learning involves a change in a person S cognitive frame of reference. It typically begins with a disorienting event, which may be either dramatic (epochal) or gradual (incremental) (Mezirow, 2003 ). In essence, transformative learning illustrates how exposure to new experiences and perspectives can result in changes in frames of reference, shifts in beliefs, and a motivation to act upon newfound understandings, collectively fostering pathways to social and structural change (Mezirow, 1991 , 1997 , 2003 ).

nodes.question: What role do social norms play in influencing food choices within supermarkets?
nodes.answer: Social norms, which consist of context-dependent, implicit, unwritten rules, influence individuals' food choices by affecting what they perceive others are doing and what they think others would approve of.
nodes.paragraph: An effective way to shift food purchases in supermarkets is through changing aspects of the food environment by means of nudging [10 12]. Nudging was introduced by Thaler and Sunstein [12] and is defined as any aspect of the choice architec - ture that alters people S behaviour in a predictable way, without forbidding any options or significantly changing their economic incentives . Nudges can be designed to target less conscious, more automatic decision-making processes, aiming to subtly disrupt habitual behaviours such as shopping behaviour at the supermarket [13]. By addressing these automatic processes, nudges can make it easier for customers to deviate from habitual behaviour and adopt alternative behaviours with rather minimal cognitive effort. Within supermarkets, individuals are steered by a vari - ety of factors in the physical and social environment. nodes.question: How does the effectiveness of social norms vary based on the majority or minority status?
nodes.answer: The effectiveness of social norms in changing behavior is greater when they are associated with the majority of a group, as in the case of "8 in 10 people eat vegetarian most days," while minority norms can have the opposite effect by suggesting that the behavior is not typical for most.
nodes.paragraph: descriptive norms) and/or prescribe what is considered appropriate by that specific referent group (i.e. injunctive norms) [17, 18]. Because of the forceful influence of social norms on food choices, social norm nudges (i.e. making social norms salient through textual communication) are deemed a promising tool to promote healthy and sustainable behaviours such as stimulating plant-based choices and/or discouraging meat choices (e.g. [1922]). The communication of social norms seems especially effective in changing behaviour when the norm regards the majority of a group (e.g. 8 in 10 people eat vegetarian most days of the week), whereas so-called minority norms (e.g. 1 in 10 people eat vegetarian most days of the week ) can have reverse effects as it implic - itly highlights that behaviour not being the normal thing to do for most of the referent group [23, 24]. Currently, reducing or abstaining from meat consumption is only done by a minority of Dutch consumers as the majority still consumes meat on five or more days of the week. In addition, only 5% of Dutch consumers are vegetarian or pescatarian [25].

nodes.label: Ethics and regulation
nodes.question: What are dynamic norms and how are they framed?
nodes.answer: Dynamic norms are social norms framed as a trend or an expected direction of a certain behavior, such as stating that a certain percentage of people are changing and reducing their meat consumption.
nodes.paragraph: Thus, communicating an absolute norm about meat reduction or abstention would result in a minority norm, risking adverse effects of such norm communication. Recently, the communication of dynamic norms is con - sidered promising to stimulate specifically behaviours that are currently not performed by the majority of a cer - tain group. Instead of framing a norm statically, dynamic norms are social norms framed as a trend or an expected direction of a certain behaviour (e.g. 5 in 10 people are now changing and reducing their meat consumption ). By framing norms dynamically rather than statically, com - municating a minority norm can be circumvented when it is a minority group that portrays the behaviour [26]. The communication of dynamic norms favouring meat reduction has shown to increase intention to reduce meat [20, 26, 27], increase meat-free orders at a caf [26, 28], and reduce self-reported weekly servings of meat [29]. However, the communication of dynamic norms favour - ing meat reduction has in some instances also resulted in no effects [30, 31] or counter-effects, reducing vegetarian orders [28].

nodes.question: How does speculative design challenge existing norms and values in society?
nodes.answer: Speculative design challenges hegemonic thoughts, norms, and values in social and political arenas by questioning the status-quo through the ambiguity of fictional objects.

nodes.question: How does Social Identity Theory (SIT) influence people's consumption behaviour?
nodes.answer: According to Blandly and Salem (2022), SIT suggests that individuals belong to various groups that influence their beliefs and consumption behaviour, allowing them to attribute meaning to action based on their perceived self-identity regardless of potential harm.
